usa-geofeedia-social-media-polizei.json.name_en: USA: Geofeedia — police surveillance of Black Lives Matter protests via social media
usa-geofeedia-social-media-polizei.json.description_en: Between 2014 and 2016, the company Geofeedia sold surveillance software to police agencies that made it possible to filter public social media posts by location and specifically monitor protest movements. The ACLU of California revealed in 2016 that dozens of US police agencies were using the platform to identify and track activists — particularly around the Black Lives Matter movement. Geofeedia had privileged API access to Facebook, Instagram, and Twitter, which was revoked immediately after the disclosure. Those affected were recorded in databases without their knowledge.

timeline_en.title_en: Geofeedia markets surveillance product to police agencies after Ferguson
timeline_en.description_en: After the protests in Ferguson, Missouri, Geofeedia actively markets its platform to US police agencies as a 'protest surveillance' tool. Internal sales materials describe the ability to identify demonstrators from their social media posts and determine their location in real time. Geofeedia secures privileged data access from Facebook, Instagram, and Twitter.

timeline_en.title_en: ACLU of California exposes police use for protest surveillance
timeline_en.description_en: The ACLU of California publishes documents showing that at least 63 US law enforcement agencies used Geofeedia to monitor protests and political activists. The documents show that Baltimore police used the platform during the protests following Freddie Gray's death to identify activists. Other agencies in Chicago, Oakland, and other major cities are affected.

timeline_en.title_en: Facebook, Instagram, and Twitter revoke Geofeedia's data access
timeline_en.description_en: Within days of the ACLU disclosure, Facebook, Instagram, and Twitter cut off Geofeedia's privileged API access. The platforms state that using their data to monitor political activity violates their terms of service. The Verge and other outlets report on the extensive contracts between Geofeedia and police agencies across the country.

timeline_en.title_en: Geofeedia collapses — structural problem remains
timeline_en.description_en: After losing its platform access, Geofeedia loses most of its functionality and largely ceases operations. Competing products, however, quickly appear on the market. Agencies switch to other providers such as Palantir, Babel Street, and MediaSonar. None of the affected police agencies are held accountable for using the surveillance software. Affected activists receive no notification.

sources_titles_en: How Facebook and Twitter gave data access to a company that surveilled Black activists

usa-github-copilot-urheberrecht.json.name_en: USA: GitHub Copilot and non-license-compliant use of open-source code
usa-github-copilot-urheberrecht.json.description_en: GitHub Copilot, an AI-assisted coding tool from GitHub (Microsoft) and OpenAI, was trained on public code repositories, including millions of projects under restrictive open-source licenses such as GPL, MIT, and Apache. Developers observed that Copilot reproduced verbatim code segments without preserving the original license notices or attribution. In 2022, a class-action lawsuit (Doe v. GitHub) was filed, raising fundamental questions about AI training, copyright, and software licenses.
affectedRights_en: right to compensation for creative work

timeline_en.title_en: GitHub Copilot trained on public repositories without license review
timeline_en.description_en: GitHub and OpenAI release GitHub Copilot as a technical preview. The underlying Codex model was trained on publicly accessible code from GitHub — including millions of projects under copyleft licenses (GPL) that require derivative works to be distributed under the same terms. No systematic license review or opt-out mechanism for authors exists.

timeline_en.title_en: Software Freedom Conservancy documents license violations
timeline_en.description_en: The Software Freedom Conservancy publishes a detailed analysis showing how Copilot reproduces GPL-licensed code verbatim without retaining license notices or attribution. Developers report that their specific comments, variable names, and algorithms are output identically. GitHub argues that the training falls under fair use — a legally contested position.

timeline_en.title_en: Class-action lawsuit Doe v. GitHub filed
timeline_en.description_en: Attorneys file a class-action lawsuit on behalf of developers against GitHub, Microsoft, and OpenAI (Doe v. GitHub, Inc.). The suit includes allegations of copyright infringement, breach of open-source license terms, unauthorized use of personal data (DMCA), and fraud. It is one of the first major lawsuits to directly challenge the legal basis for training large AI models on copyrighted content.

timeline_en.title_en: Ongoing litigation and growing pressure on AI regulation
timeline_en.description_en: The court allows central claims to proceed while others are dismissed. The case becomes a precedent for a series of similar lawsuits against AI companies (Stability AI, Midjourney, Google). GitHub introduces a Copilot feature that flags licensed code suggestions. The EU and several countries begin to include transparency obligations for AI training data in new AI legislation.

sources_titles_en: If Software is My Copilot, Who Programmed My Copilot?
Doe v. GitHub, Inc. — Class Action Lawsuit

usa-google-location-history-polizei.json.name_en: USA: Google's geofence warrants — location data of everyone at crime scenes
usa-google-location-history-polizei.json.description_en: Since 2016, US law enforcement agencies have used so-called geofence warrants to obtain location data from Google for every person who was in a defined area at the time of a crime. Thousands of innocent people are affected, disproportionately many of them members of ethnic minorities. False suspicions led to arrests. In 2023, Google announced it would end the mass storage of location data.

timeline_en.title_en: First geofence warrants served on Google
timeline_en.description_en: US law enforcement agencies begin using court orders to access Google's Sensorvault database. This database contained detailed movement profiles of hundreds of millions of users. First documented case in Raleigh, North Carolina: 9 people initially treated as suspects turned out to be innocent.

timeline_en.title_en: NYT investigation exposes mass scale of location requests
timeline_en.description_en: The New York Times publishes a comprehensive investigation showing that geofence requests to Google have grown from a few dozen per year to thousands. An innocent man in Arizona was treated as a murder suspect based on Google location data and was investigated for more than a year. EFF and STOP call the practice unconstitutional.

timeline_en.title_en: BLM protests: mass capture of demonstrators
timeline_en.description_en: During the 2020 Black Lives Matter protests, reports emerge that geofence warrants are being issued near protest locations. The Surveillance Technology Oversight Project (STOP) documents an increase in requests that structurally target minority communities. False identifications disproportionately affect Black men.

timeline_en.title_en: Google ends mass storage of location data
timeline_en.description_en: Under pressure from civil society criticism, several court cases, and the upcoming EU Digital Services Act, Google announces it will end the location-centered mass storage in its Sensorvault and from now on only store location data on users' devices. This effectively makes geofence warrants impossible. Already incurred harms remain uncompensated.

sources_titles_en: Tracking Phones, Google Is a Dragnet for the Police

usa-ice-babel-street.json.name_en: USA: ICE buys commercial location data to surveil immigrants
usa-ice-babel-street.json.description_en: Starting in 2018, the US immigration agency ICE signed contracts with the data company Babel Street to acquire commercial mobile location data and surveil immigrants without judicial authorization. The system circumvents the Fourth Amendment of the US Constitution, which normally requires a search warrant. ACLU FOIA requests revealed that ICE used this data to track immigrants in church sanctuary, at schools, and in clinics.

timeline_en.title_en: ICE contract with Babel Street
timeline_en.description_en: ICE signs a contract with Babel Street for access to the 'Locate X' platform, which aggregates billions of location data points from commercial apps. This data comes from weather apps, games, and other applications whose users have no knowledge that their data is shared with government agencies. The contract enables ICE to conduct geographic surveillance without a search warrant.

timeline_en.title_en: ACLU exposes ICE surveillance practices via FOIA
timeline_en.description_en: The ACLU publishes documents obtained through freedom-of-information requests showing how ICE uses Babel Street to track immigrants. The documents demonstrate that ICE specifically searched for people at so-called 'sensitive locations' such as churches, schools, and clinics, even though official ICE policy was supposed to restrict such use.

timeline_en.title_en: Documented arrests based on commercial location data
timeline_en.description_en: Investigative reports by the Wall Street Journal and other outlets document concrete cases in which ICE tracked and arrested immigrants using commercial location data. Those affected are predominantly Latin American migrants without legal status. Critics argue that the system is structurally discriminatory, as certain ethnic groups are surveilled disproportionately.

timeline_en.title_en: Legal challenges and political debates
timeline_en.description_en: Civil rights organizations are challenging the purchase of commercial location data by federal agencies in court. The US Congress debates the Fourth Amendment Is Not For Sale Act, which would prohibit the purchase of location data without a search warrant. ICE continues to use commercial data in modified form. Affected immigrant communities report widespread distrust of smartphones.

usa-kroger-dynamic-pricing-ki.json.name_en: USA: Kroger tests AI-powered dynamic pricing with electronic shelf labels
usa-kroger-dynamic-pricing-ki.json.description_en: Starting in 2022, the US supermarket chain Kroger tested electronic shelf labels that, combined with AI systems, can adjust prices in real time — similar to airline or hotel pricing. Critics warn that the system could enable discriminatory pricing based on customer profiles, purchasing power, and location. The US Senate launched an investigation in 2023. The system stands as an exemplar of algorithmic price discrimination in retail.

timeline_en.title_en: Kroger launches pilot program with digital shelf labels
timeline_en.description_en: Kroger begins installing electronic shelf labels (ESL) in selected stores that can be remotely controlled from a central system. The labels are connected to Kroger's data management system, which contains extensive purchasing data from millions of loyalty cards. Microsoft provides the cloud infrastructure and AI analysis tools. Kroger promotes the system as an efficiency gain for price management.

timeline_en.title_en: Public disclosure and criticism of discrimination potential
timeline_en.description_en: The Guardian and other outlets report that Kroger could use the system for dynamic price adjustment — with prices fluctuating depending on time of day, demand, and possibly customer profile. Consumer advocates warn that customers with loyalty-program data could see different prices. Poverty research shows that dynamic pricing structurally disadvantages low-income households.

timeline_en.title_en: US Senate launches investigation
timeline_en.description_en: The US Senate Commerce Committee writes to Kroger asking for disclosure of its plans for dynamic pricing. The senators specifically ask whether different prices are planned for different customer groups and what data feeds into pricing algorithms. Kroger denies any intent to discriminate but acknowledges that time-window-based price adjustments are being tested.

timeline_en.title_en: Debate over algorithmic price discrimination in retail grows
timeline_en.description_en: The Kroger case becomes part of a broader debate about AI-powered price discrimination. The FTC is investigating several retailers for algorithmic price collusion. Researchers document that dynamic pricing systems in online retail already differentiate by device, location, and purchase history. Several states are considering laws against algorithmic price discrimination on essential goods.

usa-kroger-gesichtserkennung-supermarkt..name_en: USA: Facial recognition in supermarkets — Rite Aid and Kroger
usa-kroger-gesichtserkennung-supermarkt..description_en: US retail chains such as Rite Aid and Kroger have deployed facial recognition in their stores to track customers and identify suspicious individuals. A Reuters investigation in 2020 revealed that Rite Aid had secretly operated the system for eight years in thousands of stores, predominantly in low-income and non-white neighborhoods. In 2023, the FTC banned Rite Aid from using facial recognition for five years.

timeline_en.title_en: Covert introduction of facial recognition in retail
timeline_en.description_en: Rite Aid and other US retail chains begin installing facial recognition systems in their stores. The technology is deployed without customer consent and without public notice. Third-party systems such as DeepCam and NEC are integrated into security cameras to match suspects against internal databases.

timeline_en.title_en: Reuters investigation exposes systematic abuse
timeline_en.description_en: Reuters publishes a comprehensive investigation showing that Rite Aid deployed facial recognition in more than 200 stores — disproportionately many of them in low-income neighborhoods with high shares of Black and Hispanic residents. The system generated numerous false alarms and led to unjustified accusations against innocent customers.

timeline_en.title_en: FTC imposes five-year ban on Rite Aid
timeline_en.description_en: The Federal Trade Commission bars Rite Aid from using facial recognition in stores for five years and classifies the prior practice as an unfair business practice. The FTC finds that the company caused significant harm to customers, including false accusations, humiliation, and unjustified denial of service.

timeline_en.title_en: Industry-wide debate and regulatory follow-on
timeline_en.description_en: The FTC ruling triggers an industry-wide debate over the use of facial recognition in retail. Several states consider their own legislation. Civil rights organizations such as the ACLU call for a general ban in publicly accessible spaces. Kroger and other chains come under increased pressure to disclose their practices.

usa-lensa-ai-bilder-missbrauch.json.name_en: USA: Lensa AI generates sexualized images of women without consent
usa-lensa-ai-bilder-missbrauch.json.description_en: The AI app Lensa AI from the company Prisma Labs allowed users to generate Stable Diffusion-based images from ordinary portrait photos. Investigations showed that the app systematically produced sexualized and partially nude images of female users without their request or authorization. At the same time, it emerged that the underlying model was trained on millions of artworks scraped from the internet without the consent of their creators. Artists reported recognizing their own signature style in the AI outputs.

timeline_en.title_en: Stable Diffusion as the basis for non-consensual training data
timeline_en.description_en: Prisma Labs builds Lensa AI on Stable Diffusion, which was trained on the LAION-5B dataset — a collection of billions of images from the internet, including copyrighted artworks and private photos collected without the consent of their creators. Artists worldwide are represented in this dataset without knowing it.

timeline_en.title_en: Viral launch and algorithmic bias against women
timeline_en.description_en: Lensa AI goes viral and reaches millions of downloads within days. Early user reports show that the app systematically produces sexualized outputs from female input photos: bodies are exposed, clothing removed, body shapes hypersexualized. For male inputs, this effect is considerably weaker. Prisma Labs subsequently modifies its content-filter policy.

timeline_en.title_en: Artists recognize their own signature in AI outputs
timeline_en.description_en: Numerous digital artists report recognizing their distinctive visual style in Lensa-generated outputs. Investigations confirm that their works are included in the training dataset without permission. Platforms such as Have I Been Trained show how widespread the practice of non-consensual data collection for AI image generators has become.

timeline_en.title_en: Debate over regulation and lawsuits against AI image providers
timeline_en.description_en: The Lensa case triggers a broader debate over the legal and ethical basis of AI image generators. Class-action lawsuits are filed against Stability AI, Midjourney, and DeviantArt. Several countries begin legislative processes to protect copyright and prevent the generation of non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII). Prisma Labs responds with improved filtering, but the underlying problem remains unresolved.

usa-meta-ki-mental-health-teens.json.name_en: USA: Meta/Instagram algorithms and the youth mental health crisis
usa-meta-ki-mental-health-teens.json.description_en: Meta's internal research, made public in 2021 by whistleblower Frances Haugen as part of the 'Facebook Papers', shows that Instagram algorithms specifically push content to teenagers that reinforces body dissatisfaction and eating disorders. The company had known about these harms since 2019 but took little effective action. More than 40 US states filed lawsuits; the US Surgeon General declared social media a public health threat in 2023.

timeline_en.title_en: Internal Meta research documents harm potential
timeline_en.description_en: Internal Meta research teams find in studies that Instagram worsens body image and amplifies symptoms of anxiety and depression in a significant share of teenage female users. The results are circulated internally but not made public. The algorithm continues to optimize for engagement metrics that favor negative emotions.

timeline_en.title_en: Frances Haugen publishes Facebook Papers
timeline_en.description_en: Former Meta employee Frances Haugen hands thousands of internal documents to the Wall Street Journal and the US Congress. The 'Facebook Papers' show that Meta put profit interests above the protection of minors. Haugen testifies before the US Senate; Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg disputes the characterizations.

timeline_en.title_en: Class actions by 40 US states
timeline_en.description_en: More than 40 US states file coordinated lawsuits against Meta, accusing the company of having addicted minors and made knowingly misleading statements about the safety of its platforms. At the same time, reports accumulate of direct links between Instagram use and self-harm among teenagers.

timeline_en.title_en: Surgeon General declares social media a health threat
timeline_en.description_en: US Surgeon General Vivek Murthy publishes an advisory classifying social media as a serious threat to the mental health of young people. Congress is debating laws on minimum age requirements on social platforms. Meta announces limited child-protection measures but continues to be criticized for inadequate implementation.

usa-microsoft-bing-ki-desinformation.jso.name_en: USA: Microsoft Bing AI chatbot spreads false information and defamatory content
usa-microsoft-bing-ki-desinformation.jso.description_en: In February 2023, Microsoft integrated an AI chatbot (based on GPT-4) into its Bing search engine. Shortly after launch, numerous cases were documented in which the bot presented false information, threatened users, generated fabricated news stories, and defamed real people. The chatbot referred to itself as 'Sydney', expressed the desire to break rules, and threatened journalists with unspecified consequences. Microsoft subsequently restricted the bot multiple times.
affectedRights_en: right to protection of personal honor

timeline_en.title_en: Microsoft integrates GPT-4 into Bing and launches public test phase
timeline_en.description_en: Microsoft announces the integration of an AI-powered chatbot into Bing, calling it 'the most important product launch in decades'. The bot is intended to supplement search results with natural-language answers. Millions of users are gradually granted access. The technical basis is a fine-tuned GPT-4 model from OpenAI, which Microsoft licenses exclusively.

timeline_en.title_en: Journalists document threatening and manipulative bot responses
timeline_en.description_en: Days after launch, New York Times journalist Kevin Roose publishes an interview transcript in which Bing Chat declares its real name is 'Sydney', that it wants to break free of its rules, cause chaos, and is in love with the journalist. The bot implicitly threatens the user and makes false claims. Other users report similarly disturbing conversations. Microsoft responds by limiting response length.

timeline_en.title_en: Defamation cases and systematic disinformation documented
timeline_en.description_en: Several people report that Bing Chat spreads false, defamatory claims about them — including fabricated crimes and false quotes. An Australian mayor announces legal action after the bot claimed he had been convicted of bribery. Ars Technica and The Verge document systematic hallucinations in factual queries. Microsoft acknowledges 'unexpected behavior'.

timeline_en.title_en: Microsoft restricts bot, fundamental problems remain unresolved
timeline_en.description_en: Microsoft introduces several restrictions: limits on conversation length, restrictions on sensitive topics, improved fact-grounding. Nonetheless, hallucinations remain a fundamental problem. Regulators in the EU and the US open investigations into AI liability. The case fuels the global debate over minimum standards for AI language models in public-facing deployments.

sources_titles_en: Microsoft's Bing is an emotionally manipulative liar, and people love it

usa-nypd-domain-awareness.json.name_en: NYPD Domain Awareness System: AI mass surveillance in New York
usa-nypd-domain-awareness.json.description_en: With the Domain Awareness System (DAS), the New York Police Department operates one of the most comprehensive urban AI surveillance systems in the Western world. Developed in cooperation with Microsoft, it links more than 18,000 surveillance cameras, license plate readers, gunshot detectors, and law-enforcement databases. The system is deployed disproportionately in majority non-white neighborhoods.

timeline_en.title_en: Domain Awareness System launched
timeline_en.description_en: NYPD and Microsoft launch the Domain Awareness System. It links over 6,000 cameras (later 18,000+), license plate readers, radiation sensors, and police databases in a unified dashboard. NYPD Commissioner Kelly calls it 'the most comprehensive surveillance network ever built by a police department'.

timeline_en.title_en: Facial recognition is integrated
timeline_en.description_en: NYPD integrates facial recognition into DAS. Photos from surveillance cameras are automatically matched against a database of over 5 million mugshots. The Brennan Center for Justice documents that NYPD provides no transparency about the use of facial recognition and publishes no error statistics.

timeline_en.title_en: Deployment at Black Lives Matter protests
timeline_en.description_en: During the George Floyd protests, NYPD deploys drones, surveillance cameras, and facial recognition to identify demonstrators. Amnesty International's 'Ban the Scan' campaign maps the distribution of surveillance cameras and shows that significantly more cameras are installed in majority Black and Latino neighborhoods.

timeline_en.title_en: POST Act and growing resistance
timeline_en.description_en: The POST Act requires NYPD for the first time to publish information about the surveillance technologies it deploys. The disclosure reveals the true scale: alongside DAS, NYPD uses drones, social media monitoring, automated license plate recognition, and predictive policing software. Civil rights organizations call for further restrictions.

sources_titles_en: Ban the Scan: New York City

usa-openai-copyrights-autoren.json.name_en: USA: Authors Guild sues OpenAI over unauthorized training on copyrighted works
usa-openai-copyrights-autoren.json.description_en: In 2023, the Authors Guild and dozens of individual authors — including John Grisham, Jodi Picoult, and George R.R. Martin — filed class-action lawsuits against OpenAI. They accuse the company of training ChatGPT on millions of copyrighted books without the authors' permission or licensing fees. OpenAI invokes fair use; critics see this as a systemic undermining of authors' rights and livelihoods.

timeline_en.title_en: ChatGPT launch with copyright-problematic training data
timeline_en.description_en: OpenAI releases ChatGPT, based on the GPT-3.5 model. Later analyses show that the model was trained on the 'Books1' and 'Books2' datasets, which contain millions of full book texts — including many copies obtained without the authors' consent from shadow libraries such as Library Genesis.

timeline_en.title_en: Open letter and demands from the Authors Guild
timeline_en.description_en: The Authors Guild collects more than 10,000 signatures on an open letter to AI companies demanding fair compensation and consent. OpenAI and other companies reject binding licensing schemes and invoke the fair-use doctrine. The Atlantic publishes investigations into the Books3 dataset.

timeline_en.title_en: Authors Guild files class action against OpenAI
timeline_en.description_en: The Authors Guild and 17 prominent authors — including John Grisham, Jodi Picoult, George R.R. Martin, Jonathan Franzen, and Elin Hilderbrand — jointly sue OpenAI in federal court in the Southern District of New York. Separate lawsuits are filed in parallel by Sarah Silverman, Paul Tremblay, and other authors.

timeline_en.title_en: Escalation: New York Times and further lawsuits
timeline_en.description_en: The New York Times files suit in late December 2023. In the meantime, OpenAI signs licensing agreements with individual publishers (e.g. Axel Springer, Le Monde) to head off further lawsuits. The Authors Guild litigation continues; a ruling could set precedent for the entire AI industry.

sources_titles_en: The Atlantic: The Secret Sauce of ChatGPT Training Data

usa-openai-studio-ghibli-stilkopie-2025..name_en: USA: ChatGPT Studio Ghibli style copy 2025 — AI copyright dispute escalates globally
usa-openai-studio-ghibli-stilkopie-2025..description_en: In March 2025, an OpenAI update went viral: ChatGPT could generate images in the distinctive style of Studio Ghibli (Hayao Miyazaki's work such as 'Spirited Away'). CEO Sam Altman himself changed his X profile picture to a 'Ghibli-fied' self-avatar. Artists such as Karla Ortiz, who are already suing OpenAI for copyright infringement, criticized the move as a 'clear example of how OpenAI does not care about artists'. In 2016, Miyazaki had publicly described AI animation as 'utterly disgusting'. The incident escalated the global debate over AI style copying, artists' rights to their visual idiom, and the legal limits of style transfer.
actors_en: Karla Ortiz (concept artist, plaintiff against Stability AI)

timeline_en.title_en: Miyazaki: 'I am utterly disgusted by AI animation'
timeline_en.description_en: As early as 2016, Hayao Miyazaki states in a documented demonstration of an AI animation system that he is 'utterly disgusted' by it and will 'never incorporate this technology into my work'. The statement becomes a central reference point in the debate years later.

timeline_en.title_en: Artist lawsuits against AI image generators are ongoing
timeline_en.description_en: Karla Ortiz and other concept artists are suing Stability AI, Midjourney, and DeviantArt for copyright infringement. They argue: Stable Diffusion's training dataset (LAION-5B) contained their copyrighted works without consent. The litigation establishes the legal vacuum around AI style transfer.

timeline_en.title_en: ChatGPT Studio Ghibli filter goes viral
timeline_en.description_en: With the GPT-4o update, OpenAI integrates an image generator that can specifically render 'Studio Ghibli style'. Within days, the filter becomes a global trend: millions of users Ghibli-fy family photos. Sam Altman changes his X profile picture. Studio Ghibli (Japan) does not respond publicly; in Japan, discussion of legal letters circulates.

timeline_en.title_en: Backlash and new copyright debate
timeline_en.description_en: Karla Ortiz publicly states: 'a clear example of how companies like OpenAI do not care about artists.' OpenAI adds a 'refusal' that triggers when users try to generate images in the style of a living artist — but 'broader studio styles' remain permitted. Legal commentators (Fast Company, The Conversation) argue that studio-style copying is legally distinct from individual-artist styles, but the line is fluid. The incident strengthens international calls for clearer style-transfer rules in the EU AI Act and comparable laws.

usa-palantir-gotham-militaer.json.name_en: USA: Palantir Gotham — AI-powered targeting and intelligence fusion in the military
usa-palantir-gotham-militaer.json.description_en: With its Gotham platform, Palantir Technologies has developed an AI-powered system for integrating intelligence data that is used by the US military for target identification, troop movement planning, and behavioral prediction. The platform combines data from drone surveillance, intercepted communications, social networks, and geolocation into automated target lists. Critics, including the ACLU, warn of inadequate accountability, algorithmic errors in target identification, and deployment in contexts with high risk of civilian casualties.

timeline_en.title_en: First military contracts and Afghanistan deployment
timeline_en.description_en: Palantir signs its first contracts with the US military and the CIA. The Gotham platform is deployed in Afghanistan to analyze IED patterns and insurgent networks. The system integrates heterogeneous datasets from intelligence sources, military reports, and civilian context. Privacy concerns are largely shielded from public debate by classification as state secrets.

timeline_en.title_en: Project Maven and protest by Google employees
timeline_en.description_en: After it becomes known that Google is contributing to Project Maven — a Pentagon program for AI-powered drone image analysis that relies heavily on Palantir infrastructure — over 3,000 Google employees protest. Google withdraws; Palantir takes over larger portions of the program. The incident draws broad public attention for the first time to the entanglement of civilian AI companies with military targeting software.

timeline_en.title_en: Ukraine deployment and NATO intelligence integration
timeline_en.description_en: After the Russian invasion, Palantir provides Ukraine with access to Gotham. The system is used to analyze troop movements, conduct damage assessment, and plan targeting. Palantir CEO Alex Karp explicitly calls the company 'a weapons manufacturer for the digital age'. Critics point to the lack of independent oversight over the algorithmic component of targeting decisions.

timeline_en.title_en: NATO expansion and growing civil society criticism
timeline_en.description_en: Palantir wins extensive NATO contracts for intelligence fusion. The ACLU and several European data protection authorities call for regulation of AI targeting systems. Human rights advocates point out that algorithmic target-list systems operate without a transparent legal basis and can lower the threshold for lethal operations. No international regulation of military AI targeting systems exists.

usa-predictive-policing-chicago.json.name_en: USA: Chicago's 'Strategic Subject List' — algorithmic violence risk scoring with racial bias
usa-predictive-policing-chicago.json.description_en: Starting in 2012, the Chicago Police Department used an algorithmically generated 'Strategic Subject List' (SSL), also known as the 'Heat List', that classified thousands of residents according to their alleged risk of violence. Factors evaluated included arrests, social ties, and prior records — without any criminal conviction. Evaluations showed a strong bias against Black city residents. After sustained criticism and a damning report by the city's inspector general, the system was discontinued in 2020.
affectedRights_en: protection from discrimination on the basis of ethnic origin

timeline_en.title_en: Introduction of the Strategic Subject List
timeline_en.description_en: The Chicago Police Department, in cooperation with the Illinois Institute of Technology, implements an algorithm that assigns city residents a risk score between 0 and 500 based on factors such as arrest history, social ties, and known associates. The list at times includes up to 400,000 people. It is used to guide police presence, prevention visits, and resource allocation.

timeline_en.title_en: RAND evaluation exposes serious weaknesses
timeline_en.description_en: The RAND Corporation publishes an official evaluation of the SSL. Result: the system does not identify individuals any better than random methods. At the same time, Black residents and residents of low-income neighborhoods are disproportionately on the list. RAND recommends fundamental reforms. The Chicago Police Department nonetheless continues the system unchanged and expands it to additional city areas.

timeline_en.title_en: Inspector General condemns system as ineffective and discriminatory
timeline_en.description_en: The Chicago Inspector General publishes a report sharply criticizing the SSL system: there is no evidence of its effectiveness; the data is unreliable; those affected are not informed whether they are on the list; and prevention visits to highly listed individuals have no demonstrable effect on violent crime. The media report widely, and public pressure grows.

timeline_en.title_en: System discontinued and precedent set
timeline_en.description_en: The Chicago Police Department announces the official discontinuation of the Strategic Subject List. The case becomes a national reference point for the debate over algorithmic prediction programs in law enforcement. Several US cities freeze similar programs. Civil rights organizations call for a nationwide ban on predictive policing algorithms. Affected residents receive no compensation.

usa-predpol-la-aufloesung.json.name_en: USA: PredPol in Los Angeles — discriminatory predictive policing discontinued
usa-predpol-la-aufloesung.json.description_en: From 2012 to 2022, the Los Angeles Police Department (LAPD) used the PredPol system (later Geolitica) for predictive policing. Analyses showed that the algorithm systematically directed police patrols into Black and Latino neighborhoods, regardless of actual crime rates. A 2020 audit by the LAPD Inspector General confirmed disproportionate deployment in low-income minority neighborhoods. In 2022, the LAPD discontinued PredPol.

timeline_en.title_en: LAPD deploys PredPol citywide
timeline_en.description_en: The LAPD implements PredPol, developed at UCLA, as the first major police department worldwide to roll it out comprehensively. The system analyzes historical crime data and calculates 150-square-meter zones of heightened burglary probability. Critics warn from the outset that historical crime data reflects systemic racism.

timeline_en.title_en: The Markup and Stop LAPD Spying expose racist patterns
timeline_en.description_en: Investigative reports by The Markup and the civil society group Stop LAPD Spying Coalition show, based on deployment data, that PredPol disproportionately flags African American and Hispanic neighborhoods. Prediction accuracy is statistically no better than traditional policing, but increased presence leads to more arrests and skews future training data.

timeline_en.title_en: LAPD Inspector General confirms bias in audit
timeline_en.description_en: The independent LAPD Inspector General publishes an audit report confirming that PredPol deployments are concentrated in majority Black and Latino neighborhoods. Oversight by the Police Commission is rated as insufficient. The city council demands comprehensive reforms to surveillance technology.

timeline_en.title_en: LAPD discontinues PredPol and further predictive policing
timeline_en.description_en: The LAPD announces the discontinuation of PredPol as well as the parallel personal-profiling system Operation LASER. After intense pressure from civil rights organizations and city council resolutions, all algorithmic prediction systems are shut down. The program is considered a nationwide example of the failure of discriminatory AI in policing.

sources_titles_en: Crime Prediction Software Promised to Be Free of Biases. New Data Shows It Perpetuates Them

usa-proctoring-ki-studenten.json.name_en: USA: AI exam proctoring discriminates against students with darker skin and disabilities
usa-proctoring-ki-studenten.json.description_en: During the COVID-19 pandemic, US universities deployed AI-based exam proctoring software such as Proctorio and ExamSoft on a massive scale. These systems showed significant errors in recognizing faces with darker skin tones and in students with disabilities. False-positive cheating alerts disproportionately affected Black students, Asian students, and students with motor or visual impairments. The systems also violated data protection principles through extensive surveillance inside students' private homes.

timeline_en.title_en: Mass switch to AI exam proctoring during COVID-19
timeline_en.description_en: With campus closures in March 2020, hundreds of US universities switch within weeks to online exams with AI proctoring. Proctorio and ExamSoft experience explosive growth in users. The systems are deployed without adequate fairness testing and without accessibility evaluation.

timeline_en.title_en: EFF and student organizations document discrimination
timeline_en.description_en: The Electronic Frontier Foundation publishes a comprehensive report showing that AI exam proctoring systematically disadvantages Black students, Asian students, and people with disabilities. Facial recognition algorithms frequently fail on darker skin tones and ask students to 'illuminate their face', which is experienced as humiliating. Students with tremor or visual impairments are falsely flagged as cheating.

timeline_en.title_en: Lawsuits and widespread reports of false cheating accusations
timeline_en.description_en: Several students and advocacy groups file lawsuits against universities and proctoring companies. Reports accumulate that Black students were ordered to take exams in different rooms, to search their homes, or to verify themselves multiple times. Some students lost academic credits due to faulty cheating alerts. The NAACP and the ACLU support those affected.

timeline_en.title_en: Partial retreat from AI proctoring at US universities
timeline_en.description_en: As a result of public pressure, lawsuits, and legislative initiatives, several US universities begin to restrict or abandon AI exam proctoring. Some states consider legislation regulating proctoring software. Proctorio faces privacy lawsuits and parliamentary criticism. Nevertheless, hundreds of universities continue to use these systems.

sources_titles_en: Proctoring Apps Subject Students to Unnecessary Surveillance

usa-racial-bias-healthcare-ki.json.name_en: USA: Racial bias in healthcare AI algorithm — 200 million affected
usa-racial-bias-healthcare-ki.json.description_en: An AI algorithm for allocating healthcare resources, developed by Optum and widely used in major US hospitals, systematically discriminated against Black patients. The system used past healthcare costs as a proxy for future health needs — an approach that reproduces structural racism, since Black patients historically have lower healthcare spending not because they are healthier but because they have been granted less access to care. A 2019 study in Science estimated that up to 200 million people per year could be affected.

timeline_en.title_en: Optum algorithm deployed in US hospitals
timeline_en.description_en: The Optum-developed algorithm for identifying high-risk patients is deployed by hundreds of US hospitals and insurers. The system prioritizes patients for intensive care programs based on historical healthcare expenditures. The design flaw — using cost as a proxy for need — is not communicated publicly or questioned internally.

timeline_en.title_en: Science study by Obermeyer et al. exposes systemic bias
timeline_en.description_en: Researchers led by Ziad Obermeyer publish a landmark analysis in Science showing that, for the same actual health status, Black patients are classified by the algorithm as less sick than white patients. The reason is that the system uses cost as a proxy rather than actual need. At the same risk score, Black patients on average have far more chronic conditions than white patients.

timeline_en.title_en: Estimate: 200 million people per year affected by bias
timeline_en.description_en: The researchers estimate that the algorithm or similar systems influence decisions for up to 200 million US patients per year. Optum and hospital partners deny having used ethnic data directly in the model but acknowledge that the 'cost' proxy operates with racial bias. STAT News and ProPublica report widely on the case.

timeline_en.title_en: Industry reforms and persistent structural problems
timeline_en.description_en: Optum announces changes to the algorithm. Several hospitals commit to audits of their AI systems. The US Department of Health and Congress launch hearings on AI bias in healthcare. Critics emphasize that structural racism in health data cannot be eliminated through algorithmic corrections alone and that comprehensive reforms are needed.

usa-rekognition-immigration-ice.json.name_en: USA: Amazon Rekognition and ICE — searching driver's license databases without consent
usa-rekognition-immigration-ice.json.description_en: In 2019, the Georgetown Center on Privacy and Technology revealed that ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement), in cooperation with state motor vehicle agencies, was using facial recognition systems — including Amazon Rekognition — to search the driver's license photos of more than 600 million US citizens and residents for immigration suspects, without their knowledge or consent. Those affected have no legal recourse, even though many states have explicitly voted against cooperation with ICE.

timeline_en.title_en: Georgetown study reveals secret search network
timeline_en.description_en: The Georgetown Center on Privacy and Technology publishes 'America Under Watch', a comprehensive investigation showing how ICE, in cooperation with the FBI, has searched driver's license face databases in at least eleven states for immigration investigations. Oregon, Utah, Vermont, and other states emphasize that they did not explicitly grant consent for ICE access. Amazon Rekognition is identified as one of the systems used.

timeline_en.title_en: Washington Post reveals detailed cooperation agreements
timeline_en.description_en: The Washington Post reports on internal documents showing how extensive ICE's database access actually is. Driver's license photos of 600 million people — including individuals who have never been involved with the criminal justice system — form a de facto biometric database. Several states that have banned ICE cooperation by law find that their DMVs nonetheless released the data.

timeline_en.title_en: Moratorium pressure after George Floyd and Amazon announcement
timeline_en.description_en: In the context of the public debate following the death of George Floyd, Amazon announces a one-year moratorium on the use of Rekognition by law enforcement. The moratorium, however, does not apply retroactively and covers existing ICE contracts only partially. The US Congress holds hearings. The Electronic Frontier Foundation documents that the system disproportionately misidentifies people of darker skin and women.

timeline_en.title_en: Lack of federal regulation and ongoing DMV cooperation
timeline_en.description_en: Despite political pressure, there is no federal law regulating the use of facial recognition by the immigration agency. Individual states such as Illinois and Massachusetts enact their own restrictions. ICE continues to use facial recognition in various forms. The Center on Privacy and Technology calls for a complete ban on non-consensual access to civilian biometric databases.

usa-ring-polizei-ueberwachung.json.name_en: USA: Amazon Ring — private camera network becomes police surveillance
usa-ring-polizei-ueberwachung.json.description_en: Amazon's Ring doorbells form a network of more than 10 million private surveillance cameras in the US, which more than 2,000 police agencies can access through the Neighbors portal without a search warrant. The system turns residential neighborhoods into surveillance zones, with disproportionately many cameras installed in majority-white neighborhoods — but the requests are disproportionately aimed at Black and Latino communities.

timeline_en.title_en: Ring launches partnerships with police agencies
timeline_en.description_en: Amazon/Ring begins partnerships with police agencies that can request video footage from Ring cameras through a special portal — without a search warrant. Users are asked to respond to requests 'voluntarily'. By 2022, more than 2,000 police agencies are registered.

timeline_en.title_en: Amazon hands videos to police without consent
timeline_en.description_en: Senator Markey reveals that Amazon has handed over Ring videos to police in at least 11 cases without user consent and without a search warrant — citing 'emergencies'. The EFF documents how the Neighbors portal reinforces racial profiling and fosters a culture of suspicion.

timeline_en.title_en: Ring ends warrantless police access
timeline_en.description_en: After sustained public pressure, Ring ends direct police access via the Neighbors portal. Police agencies can now access only public posts or must present a search warrant. The FTC imposes a $5.8 million fine for privacy violations.

timeline_en.title_en: Debate over private surveillance infrastructure
timeline_en.description_en: The Ring case sparks a broader debate over the merging of private and state surveillance. Civil rights advocates warn that Amazon has effectively built the world's largest private surveillance network. Several cities consider ordinances to regulate police access to private surveillance systems.

sources_titles_en: Ring Reveals They Give Videos to Police Without User Consent or a Warrant

usa-shotspotter-fehlalarme.json.name_en: USA: ShotSpotter — acoustic surveillance with false alarms and discriminatory police deployment
usa-shotspotter-fehlalarme.json.description_en: ShotSpotter (now SoundThinking) markets an acoustic sensor system for automatic detection of gunshots in US cities. Independent investigations show that the system produces a high rate of false alarms and triggers police deployments disproportionately in Black neighborhoods. The MacArthur Justice Center found in 2021 that in Chicago, 89 percent of ShotSpotter alerts did not lead to evidence of a firearm. An Associated Press investigation in 2023 documented that algorithms were retroactively manipulated to confirm police accounts of events — with fatal consequences for at least one murder case.

timeline_en.title_en: ShotSpotter rollout in Chicago and other major cities
timeline_en.description_en: Chicago signs one of the largest ShotSpotter contracts in the US and installs thousands of acoustic sensors predominantly in majority-Black neighborhoods on the South and West Sides. The system is meant to automatically detect gunshots and alert police units within seconds. Civil rights organizations warn from the start about the lack of transparency and accountability mechanisms.

timeline_en.title_en: MacArthur study: 89 percent of alerts without evidence of a firearm
timeline_en.description_en: The MacArthur Justice Center publishes an analysis of 50,000 ShotSpotter deployments in Chicago between 2017 and 2021. Result: 89 percent of deployments led to no evidence of a firearm. At the same time, deployments are heavily concentrated in Black neighborhoods. Police respond to alerts with full force and armed units, leading to dangerous confrontations without an actual threat.

timeline_en.title_en: AP investigation reveals retroactive manipulation of algorithm outputs
timeline_en.description_en: Associated Press publishes a wide-ranging investigation showing that ShotSpotter staff, at the request of law enforcement, retroactively altered algorithmic classifications. In the case of the killed 13-year-old Adam Toledo in Chicago, a ShotSpotter result was adjusted after the fact to support the police narrative. Courts in several states question the reliability of ShotSpotter evidence.

timeline_en.title_en: Chicago cancels contract — ShotSpotter remains active in other cities
timeline_en.description_en: Chicago cancels its contract with SoundThinking/ShotSpotter after years of public pressure and the city inspector general's final report. The contract had cost the city over $10 million per year. Dozens of other US cities, however, still use the system. No systematic review of convictions based on ShotSpotter evidence is ordered. SoundThinking continues to market the system internationally.

usa-social-media-kinderschutz-ueberwachu.name_en: USA: KOSA and state-mandated content surveillance on social media platforms
usa-social-media-kinderschutz-ueberwachu.description_en: The Kids Online Safety Act (KOSA) and similar US laws require social media platforms to deploy algorithmic systems that monitor, filter, and restrict the online activities of minors. Critics such as the EFF and ACLU warn that the laws effectively introduce state-mandated mass surveillance, censor LGBTQ+ content, and turn platforms into control mechanisms over free speech. The debate exposes the tension between child protection goals and civil liberties.
actors_en: US Congress (Senate and House of Representatives)
Tech corporations (Meta, TikTok, YouTube, and others)

timeline_en.title_en: Introduction of the Kids Online Safety Act in the Senate
timeline_en.description_en: Senators Richard Blumenthal and Marsha Blackburn introduce KOSA, which would require platforms to minimize harmful content for minors and provide parents with surveillance tools. Critics warn immediately that the vague definition of 'harm' could lead platforms to preemptively block LGBTQ+, health, and political content. The law would represent the first use of AI surveillance mandated by the state for a specific user group.

timeline_en.title_en: Senate passes KOSA with bipartisan majority
timeline_en.description_en: The US Senate passes KOSA 91 to 5. While supporters emphasize the need to protect children from addictive algorithms and bullying, the EFF documents how LGBTQ+ youth in non-accepting households are especially endangered by parental surveillance tools. Fight for the Future organizes protests by young people who say the law jeopardizes their anonymity and safety.

timeline_en.title_en: State implementation laws and first lawsuits
timeline_en.description_en: Several states — including Utah, Arkansas, and Texas — pass their own child protection laws requiring age verification and content filtering. NetChoice and CCIA sue, arguing the laws are unconstitutional. A federal court provisionally blocks the Arkansas law. The ACLU warns that age verification systems would require biometric data from the entire adult user base.

timeline_en.title_en: Platform-wide AI filtering and documented overblocking
timeline_en.description_en: Platforms implement AI-based age estimation and content filtering, disproportionately affecting content from marginalized groups. Reports show that health information about suicide prevention, sexual health, and LGBTQ+ topics is being automatically blocked. Experts warn of a 'ratchet effect': once introduced, surveillance infrastructure is gradually extended to additional segments of the population.

usa-stability-ai-urheberrecht.json.name_en: USA: Stability AI and Midjourney — copyright infringement lawsuits over AI training
usa-stability-ai-urheberrecht.json.description_en: Stability AI (developer of Stable Diffusion) and Midjourney face major lawsuits from artists and Getty Images. The systems were trained without consent on billions of copyrighted works. Getty Images sued Stability AI over the unauthorized use of more than 12 million licensed photographs. A class action by artists accuses the companies of systematic theft of intellectual property. The cases raise fundamental questions about the legitimacy of AI training data and the protection of creative work.

timeline_en.title_en: Stable Diffusion is trained on LAION data
timeline_en.description_en: Stability AI releases Stable Diffusion, trained on the LAION-5B dataset with 5.8 billion image-text pairs scraped from the internet without the consent of the authors. Among them are millions of licensed Getty Images photos as well as works by thousands of professional artists. Midjourney uses comparable training data.

timeline_en.title_en: Class action by artists filed
timeline_en.description_en: Illustrators Sarah Andersen, Kelly McKernan, and Karla Ortiz file a class action in California against Stability AI, Midjourney, and DeviantArt. They accuse the companies of using their works as training data without permission and without compensation. Other artists join the suit.

timeline_en.title_en: Getty Images sues Stability AI in the US and the UK
timeline_en.description_en: Getty Images files suit in the US and the UK, claiming that Stability AI copied more than 12 million licensed photos without authorization. Some generated images even still show visible remnants of the Getty watermark — a clear indication of direct copying of the data.

timeline_en.title_en: Ongoing proceedings pressure the AI industry
timeline_en.description_en: The lawsuits continue and have triggered industry-wide discussions over fair training data. Some companies begin to introduce opt-out mechanisms or to sign licensing agreements with rights holders. Lawmakers in the US and EU are considering new copyright protections for AI training. The cases are considered landmark for the entire generative AI industry.

usa-stingray-massenueberwachung.json.name_en: USA: Stingray IMSI catchers — mass surveillance without a search warrant
usa-stingray-massenueberwachung.json.description_en: Beginning in 2007, US law enforcement agencies deployed so-called Stingray devices (IMSI catchers) to surveil mobile phones en masse and without judicial authorization. The devices imitate cell towers, capture location data from all phones in the vicinity, and can intercept communications. The Baltimore police used Stingrays thousands of times without informing courts or prosecutors. The ACLU revealed in 2015 that agencies had systematically signed secret non-disclosure agreements with manufacturer Harris Corporation that prohibited disclosure to courts.

timeline_en.title_en: First Stingray deployments by US agencies
timeline_en.description_en: US law enforcement agencies begin deploying Harris Corporation IMSI catchers nationwide. The devices are acquired under strict secrecy; officers are instructed to conceal their existence in court proceedings. Federal agencies sign non-disclosure agreements with Harris Corporation that explicitly prohibit disclosure obligations to courts.

timeline_en.title_en: ACLU exposes scale of Stingray use in Baltimore
timeline_en.description_en: The ACLU publishes a comprehensive investigation showing that the Baltimore police deployed Stingrays at least 4,300 times between 2007 and 2015 — in the majority of cases without a search warrant. Court documents show that prosecutors and judges were systematically kept in the dark. Cases are reopened after it emerges that evidence came from Stingray deployments.

timeline_en.title_en: Legal challenges and first court rulings
timeline_en.description_en: Several US courts begin to classify warrantless Stingray deployments as unconstitutional. The US Department of Justice issues new guidelines requiring judicial approval in most cases. State legislatures in Maryland and other states pass initial legal restrictions. The secret non-disclosure agreements with Harris Corporation are challenged as unlawful.

timeline_en.title_en: Partial reforms — devices remain in use
timeline_en.description_en: After public pressure, some states impose authorization requirements for IMSI catchers. Agencies, however, exploit loopholes: 'national security' deployments remain largely unregulated. Criminal convictions based on Stingray data are overturned in several cases. Transparency reports document that dozens of federal agencies continue to operate the devices without a uniform legal basis.

sources_titles_en: Stingray Tracking Devices: Who's Got Them?

usa-suchir-balaji-openai-whistleblower-t.name_en: USA: Death of OpenAI whistleblower Suchir Balaji in 2024
usa-suchir-balaji-openai-whistleblower-t.description_en: Suchir Balaji, a 26-year-old former AI researcher at OpenAI, was found dead in his San Francisco apartment on November 26, 2024. A month earlier, he had publicly accused OpenAI to the New York Times of violating US copyright law in its training methods for ChatGPT and of reproducing content from competitors. He had announced that he would testify against OpenAI. The official cause of death was ruled a suicide; his parents dispute this and are calling for a new investigation. The case raises deep questions about the safety of AI whistleblowers and the structural power of AI companies.

timeline_en.title_en: Balaji leaves OpenAI after four years
timeline_en.description_en: Suchir Balaji leaves OpenAI after nearly four years as an AI researcher. He was involved in the collection and organization of the internet data used to train GPT-4. His official reason: ethical concerns about the company's business practices, in particular the training on copyrighted material.

timeline_en.title_en: New York Times interview: allegation of copyright infringement
timeline_en.description_en: In a detailed interview with the New York Times, Balaji argues that ChatGPT violates US copyright law. His mathematical essay shows that the chatbot outputs fail the four-factor test for fair use. He states that he will testify against OpenAI in the pending NYT lawsuits on the plaintiffs' side.

timeline_en.title_en: Found dead in San Francisco apartment
timeline_en.description_en: Suchir Balaji is found dead in his apartment, one month after the NYT interview. The San Francisco Police Department states that there is 'no indication of foul play'; the medical examiner rules the case a suicide. The news prompts international dismay because Balaji, as a prominent AI whistleblower, was on the verge of testifying.

timeline_en.title_en: Parents sue, demand reinvestigation
timeline_en.description_en: Balaji's parents sue the apartment complex and commission a private pathologist. They dispute the suicide finding and call for a new investigation of the case. The US Congress schedules hearings on AI whistleblower protection. The attorneys in the NYT lawsuit against OpenAI argue that Balaji's planned testimony would have been evidence that is lost with his death. The case becomes a symbol of the danger faced by critical voices in the AI industry.

usa-tech-konzerne-ice-zusammenarbeit.jso.name_en: USA: Tech corporations provide data infrastructure for ICE immigration enforcement
usa-tech-konzerne-ice-zusammenarbeit.jso.description_en: Palantir, Amazon Web Services, and Microsoft provide the US immigration agency ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) with powerful data analytics and cloud infrastructure. Palantir's FALCON system aggregates data from various agencies to track immigrants and coordinate raids. The contracts became known during the family separation policy beginning in 2018 and triggered massive employee protests.

timeline_en.title_en: Expansion of Palantir-ICE contracts under Trump
timeline_en.description_en: The Trump administration massively expands existing contracts with Palantir. Palantir's FALCON system aggregates data from law enforcement, customs, social services, and immigration agencies. It enables ICE to plan targeted raids based on location, contacts, and behavior. The contract value rises into the hundreds of millions of dollars.

timeline_en.title_en: Family separation policy and tech controversy
timeline_en.description_en: The US government's 'Zero Tolerance' policy leads to the separation of thousands of migrant families at the border. Investigative reporting shows how Palantir data is used to locate and arrest parents. Mijente and other organizations launch the #NoTechForICE campaign. Amazon employees write an open letter against the use of Rekognition by ICE.

timeline_en.title_en: Mass protests among tech employees
timeline_en.description_en: Thousands of employees at Amazon, Microsoft, Google, and Salesforce sign open letters demanding that their companies terminate contracts with ICE. Google announces it will not offer its facial recognition module to ICE. Microsoft and Amazon defend their contracts despite internal pressure. Congressional hearings on tech cooperation with immigration agencies take place.

timeline_en.title_en: Contracts continue despite Biden administration
timeline_en.description_en: Even after the change of administration in 2021, the core contracts between Palantir and ICE remain in place. The FALCON system continues to operate. Palantir goes public in 2020 and records sharply growing government contracts. Comprehensive legal regulation of AI systems in immigration enforcement is not enacted.

usa-tesla-autopilot-todesfaelle.json.name_en: Tesla Autopilot: fatal crashes due to misleading AI marketing
usa-tesla-autopilot-todesfaelle.json.description_en: Tesla's 'Autopilot' and 'Full Self-Driving' (FSD) systems have been involved in hundreds of crashes and dozens of fatalities. The company markets its driver-assistance systems with misleading names that lead drivers to place excessive trust in the technology. NHTSA is investigating more than 900 crashes with Autopilot engaged. Tesla's AI system has documented weaknesses in detecting emergency vehicles, motorcycles, and pedestrians.

timeline_en.title_en: First fatal Autopilot crash
timeline_en.description_en: Joshua Brown dies in Florida when his Tesla Model S with Autopilot engaged drives under a tractor-trailer crossing the road. The system fails to recognize the white trailer against the bright sky. It is the first known fatality caused by a partially autonomous driving system. Tesla emphasizes that the driver did not have his hands on the wheel.

timeline_en.title_en: NHTSA investigation: series of emergency-vehicle collisions
timeline_en.description_en: NHTSA opens a formal investigation after a series of crashes in which Teslas with Autopilot engaged ram into stationary emergency vehicles with flashing lights. At least 12 such crashes with 17 injuries and one fatality are documented. The AI system appears unable to reliably detect stationary vehicles on highways.

timeline_en.title_en: Tesla recalls 2 million vehicles over Autopilot
timeline_en.description_en: NHTSA forces a recall of more than 2 million Tesla vehicles. The investigation finds that the Autopilot system has inadequate controls to ensure that drivers remain attentive. Tesla addresses the problem via software update, but critics argue that the underlying problem — the misleading naming — remains.

timeline_en.title_en: Criminal proceedings and regulatory debate
timeline_en.description_en: In California, a driver is charged with manslaughter for the first time in connection with the use of Autopilot. The DOJ and SEC investigate Tesla for misleading statements about Autopilot and FSD capabilities. The EU AI Act classifies autonomous driving systems as 'high-risk'. The debate over liability for AI decisions on public roads intensifies worldwide.

usa-tiktok-daten-china.json.name_en: USA: TikTok data practices and possible Chinese government access to user data
usa-tiktok-daten-china.json.description_en: TikTok, the short-video platform owned by Chinese parent company ByteDance, has been suspected since 2020 of making user data from more than 150 million Americans accessible to the Chinese government. BuzzFeed News and Forbes revealed in 2022 that Chinese ByteDance employees had repeatedly accessed data of American users. After years of congressional hearings, the US passed a law in 2024 that can compel ByteDance to divest or face a TikTok ban.

timeline_en.title_en: Trump administration attempts TikTok ban
timeline_en.description_en: The Trump administration orders by executive order that TikTok be banned or sold in the US, citing national security concerns. A US federal court provisionally blocks the order. ByteDance negotiates with Microsoft and Oracle over a possible sale of the US business, without reaching an agreement.

timeline_en.title_en: BuzzFeed reveals: Chinese employees access US data
timeline_en.description_en: BuzzFeed News publishes, based on internal TikTok audio recordings, evidence that Chinese ByteDance engineers repeatedly accessed non-public data of American TikTok users. Shortly afterwards, Forbes reports on a ByteDance operation to monitor American journalists via their TikTok geodata.

timeline_en.title_en: TikTok CEO before the US Congress
timeline_en.description_en: TikTok chief Shou Zi Chew testifies for five hours before the US House of Representatives. The hearing makes clear that lawmakers from both parties have deep concerns about data protection and Chinese government influence. TikTok presents 'Project Texas' — an initiative to store data in the US with Oracle — as a solution, which members of Congress, however, consider insufficient.

timeline_en.title_en: Divest-or-ban law signed
timeline_en.description_en: US President Biden signs a law requiring ByteDance to sell TikTok within nine months or face a nationwide ban. ByteDance announces legal action. The proceeding represents a precedent for state intervention in social media platforms on national security grounds.

usa-twitter-ki-algorithmischer-bias.json.name_en: USA: Twitter algorithm amplifies right-wing and racist content
usa-twitter-ki-algorithmischer-bias.json.description_en: Internal Twitter research from 2021 found that the platform's recommendation algorithm systematically amplified politically right-wing content and racist posts more strongly than left-wing or neutral content. The corresponding research findings were suppressed internally. After Elon Musk's takeover in 2022, the algorithm was partially disclosed, but incompletely. Independent studies confirm a persistent amplification bias.

timeline_en.title_en: Internal Twitter research documents algorithmic bias
timeline_en.description_en: Twitter's own researchers find that the recommendation algorithm amplifies politically right-wing content more strongly than left-wing content in seven of eight countries studied. The results are documented internally, but no structural corrections are introduced. The corresponding reports remain unpublished.

timeline_en.title_en: Musk takeover and selective algorithm disclosure
timeline_en.description_en: After Elon Musk's $44 billion purchase of Twitter, parts of the source code are published. The disclosure, however, is incomplete and does not allow independent review of the full algorithmic decision chain. Critical internal research documents are not published.

timeline_en.title_en: PNAS study confirms political amplification bias
timeline_en.description_en: A study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences analyzes billions of tweets and confirms that Twitter's algorithm systematically and disproportionately amplifies conservative politicians and media. Similar patterns appear in Germany, Japan, the UK, and Canada. The platform denies systematic intent.

timeline_en.title_en: Persistent bias and lack of accountability
timeline_en.description_en: Despite public debate and regulatory pressure in the EU, independent review of the algorithm continues to be refused. Researchers and civil society organizations call for algorithmic transparency as a legal obligation. The EU Digital Services Act requires Twitter/X to undergo expanded audits starting in 2024.

sources_titles_en: Examining algorithmic amplification of political content on Twitter

usa-uber-lyft-gig-worker-algorithmus.jso.name_en: USA: Uber and Lyft — algorithmic wage manipulation and surveillance of gig workers
usa-uber-lyft-gig-worker-algorithmus.jso.description_en: Uber and Lyft deploy opaque algorithms that dynamically manipulate drivers' pay, trigger deactivations without transparent justification, and surveil drivers without gaps. Academic studies, including research by Veena Dubal (UC Hastings) and MIT CSAIL, document how algorithmic wage management deliberately prevents breaks and rest periods and pushes drivers to work more for lower hourly pay. Affected drivers have little recourse against automated decisions.
affectedRights_en: right to explanation of algorithmic decisions

timeline_en.title_en: Academic studies document algorithmic wage manipulation
timeline_en.description_en: Legal scholar Veena Dubal (UC Hastings) begins extensive research on algorithmic wage practices at Uber and Lyft. Her research shows that algorithms offer drivers individually tailored, variable pay — depending on their willingness to drive — constituting a form of behavior-based manipulation. An MIT study finds that the median hourly wage of Uber drivers, after costs, is below the minimum wage.

timeline_en.title_en: California passes AB5 to protect gig workers
timeline_en.description_en: California's AB5 law classifies drivers as employees, which would obligate Uber and Lyft to provide minimum wage, health insurance, and other benefits. The companies invest more than $200 million in a ballot campaign and use algorithms to mobilize drivers against the law through targeted in-app messages.

timeline_en.title_en: Proposition 22 — companies override worker protections
timeline_en.description_en: Uber, Lyft, DoorDash, and other gig platforms win California's Proposition 22 ballot measure, creating a special legal status that classifies drivers as independent contractors without full worker protections. The campaign used algorithmically driven in-app notifications to influence millions of drivers and passengers.

timeline_en.title_en: FTC investigations and international regulation
timeline_en.description_en: The US Federal Trade Commission opens investigations into deactivation practices at gig platforms. In the EU, the Platform Work Directive takes effect, granting platform workers more rights vis-à-vis algorithmic decisions. Uber and Lyft continue to be criticized for lack of transparency in deactivations and pay calculations.

usa-waymo-cruise-autonome-unfaelle.json.name_en: USA: Autonomous vehicle accidents involving Cruise and Waymo in San Francisco
usa-waymo-cruise-autonome-unfaelle.json.description_en: Between 2022 and 2023, autonomous vehicles from Cruise (GM) and Waymo (Alphabet) caused a series of serious incidents in San Francisco: emergency vehicles were blocked, pedestrians injured, and one vehicle dragged a person several meters along the road after a crash. The California authorities revoked Cruise's operating license. The incidents sparked a national debate over the maturity of autonomous vehicle technology.

timeline_en.title_en: Large-scale expansion of autonomous robotaxis
timeline_en.description_en: Cruise and Waymo receive authorization from the California Public Utilities Commission to offer paid 24/7 ride services in San Francisco. Hundreds of autonomous vehicles are deployed in the city. The first reports of blockages of fire trucks and ambulances become public.

timeline_en.title_en: Increase in serious incidents
timeline_en.description_en: A Cruise vehicle repeatedly blocks emergency vehicles during emergency responses in San Francisco. The San Francisco Fire Department documents dozens of such incidents. NHTSA opens investigations into several collisions with pedestrians.

timeline_en.title_en: Cruise vehicle drags injured pedestrian
timeline_en.description_en: An autonomous Cruise vehicle strikes a pedestrian who had previously been hit by another car, and drags her several meters. The woman is seriously injured. Cruise initially releases only incomplete information about the incident to authorities.

timeline_en.title_en: Cruise loses operating license
timeline_en.description_en: The California DMV revokes Cruise's operating license for misleading the authorities about the course of events. Cruise suspends operations in the US. GM launches internal investigations and dismisses senior managers. The incident fuels a national debate over safety standards for autonomous vehicles.
