usa-ziprecruiter-ki-diskriminierung.json.name_en: USA: AI hiring platforms discriminate by accent, appearance, and disability
usa-ziprecruiter-ki-diskriminierung.json.description_en: AI-driven hiring platforms such as ZipRecruiter and HireVue have been criticized as discriminating against applicants with non-Anglo-American accents, atypical appearance, and disabilities. HireVue analyzed video interviews automatically using facial recognition and voice analysis, reproducing structural biases from training data. The US privacy organization EPIC filed a complaint with the FTC in 2020. HireVue discontinued facial analysis in 2021, but voice analysis and algorithmic selection remain in use and are barely regulated.

timeline_en.title_en: HireVue deploys automated video analysis
timeline_en.description_en: HireVue uses an AI system that automatically evaluates applicants' video interviews based on facial expressions, eye movements, speech melody, and word choice. More than 700 companies, including Goldman Sachs and Unilever, deploy the system. Critics warn that the model is based on predominantly white, English-speaking training data and therefore produces systematic bias.

timeline_en.title_en: EPIC files FTC complaint
timeline_en.description_en: The Electronic Privacy Information Center (EPIC) files a formal complaint with the US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) against HireVue. EPIC accuses the company of using a 'black box' AI that evaluates applicants based on features that have no valid basis for hiring decisions. Disabilities, accents, and ethnically associated facial features are identified as potential sources of discrimination.

timeline_en.title_en: HireVue discontinues facial analysis
timeline_en.description_en: Under pressure from privacy organizations and critical reporting, HireVue announces it will remove facial analysis from its system. The company disputes that the system is flawed but cites lack of public trust as its reason. Voice analysis and algorithmic scoring remain active. ZipRecruiter and comparable platforms, meanwhile, continue algorithmic preselection without comparable public scrutiny.

timeline_en.title_en: EEOC guidance and persistent regulatory gap
timeline_en.description_en: The US Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) publishes guidance on AI discrimination in hiring, but provides no enforcement mechanisms. Studies show that applicants with non-Anglo-American accents and visible disabilities continue to be systematically disadvantaged by AI systems. Comprehensive federal regulation of hiring AI does not materialize.

sources_titles_en: In re HireVue — Complaint, Request for Investigation and Injunction
EEOC Guidance on Artificial Intelligence and Equal Employment Opportunity

usbekistan-ki-smart-city-ueberwachung.js.name_en: Uzbekistan: Huawei Safe City and AI surveillance in Tashkent
usbekistan-ki-smart-city-ueberwachung.js.description_en: Since 2019, Uzbekistan has deployed Huawei's Safe City system in Tashkent, encompassing facial recognition, AI-powered video surveillance, and centralized data management. The system is presented as a modernization measure but poses substantial risks to civil society in a state rated 'Not Free' by Freedom House. During the 2022 Karakalpakstan protests, the system was apparently used to identify demonstrators.

timeline_en.title_en: Contract signed and start of Safe City implementation
timeline_en.description_en: The Uzbek government signs a contract with Huawei for the implementation of a Safe City system for Tashkent. The system includes thousands of cameras with AI video analytics, facial recognition, and a central command center. Huawei promotes the project as part of its global smart city export strategy. There is no transparency about the system's exact capabilities or data-protection measures.

timeline_en.title_en: Expansion to additional cities and integration into the security apparatus
timeline_en.description_en: The system is expanded to additional major cities in Uzbekistan. The density of cameras in Tashkent rises sharply. The Ministry of the Interior integrates Safe City into its operational infrastructure. Privacy International and RFE/RL report on the system but cannot fully document its capabilities due to lack of transparency.

timeline_en.title_en: Karakalpakstan protests: suspected use to identify demonstrators
timeline_en.description_en: During major protests in the autonomous Republic of Karakalpakstan against planned constitutional changes, demonstrators are identified and arrested. Observers suspect the use of facial recognition systems but cannot directly prove it due to lack of transparency. Dozens of demonstrators are sentenced to long prison terms. Internet connections are temporarily throttled.

timeline_en.title_en: Expansion of surveillance infrastructure without reform pressure
timeline_en.description_en: Uzbekistan continues to expand its smart city infrastructure. Critical voices on domestic surveillance are suppressed. International investors and trade partners do not publicly raise data-protection concerns. Freedom House continues to rate Uzbekistan as 'Not Free'. The system is considered a model for other Central Asian states.

sources_titles_en: Freedom in the World: Uzbekistan

venezuela-patria-ueberwachung.json.name_en: Venezuela: Patria platform and Chinese-style social control system
venezuela-patria-ueberwachung.json.description_en: Venezuela has built a digital social control system with support from ZTE (China), operating via the so-called 'Patria' platform and the 'Carnet de la Patria' (Fatherland Card). The system links identity, access to state benefits (food subsidies, social benefits), voting behavior, and political loyalty. Reuters revealed in 2018 that ZTE provided the technical infrastructure. The system enables surveillance of movements, communications, and political activity, with access to essential goods made dependent on participation in the system.

timeline_en.title_en: Introduction of the Carnet de la Patria
timeline_en.description_en: President Nicolás Maduro introduces the 'Carnet de la Patria', a digital ID card tied to a mobile platform. Biometric data, address, family status, and political party affiliation are captured. The system is presented as voluntary, but access to state benefits is increasingly tied to it. ZTE provides technology and infrastructure.

timeline_en.title_en: Reuters revelation: ZTE replicates China's surveillance model
timeline_en.description_en: Reuters publishes a comprehensive investigation documenting that ZTE helped build a data system modeled on China's social credit system. The system tracks political activities, purchasing behavior, and mobility. During elections, the card is scanned at polling stations — government officials deny that voting data is linked to benefit eligibility, but eyewitnesses report the opposite.

timeline_en.title_en: COVID tracking and expansion of the platform
timeline_en.description_en: During the COVID-19 pandemic, the Patria platform is used to distribute food (CLAP boxes), gas cylinders, and direct payments. Reports by Access Now and human rights organizations show that opposition supporters and protest participants are systematically disadvantaged in benefit allocation. The platform thereby becomes an instrument of political discipline over the population.

timeline_en.title_en: Election surveillance and international pressure
timeline_en.description_en: At the 2023 regional elections, the Carnet de la Patria is deployed comprehensively at polling stations. International election observers criticize the lack of transparency. The US and EU impose sanctions on ZTE contracts with Venezuela. Human rights advocates note that the system could serve as a model for other authoritarian governments in Latin America. Domestic dissent is effectively suppressed by denial of access to benefits.

Freedom in the World 2023: Venezuela

vietnam-ki-zensur-firewall.json.name_en: Vietnam: AI-powered internet censorship and Cybersecurity Law
vietnam-ki-zensur-firewall.json.description_en: Vietnam uses AI-powered systems to automate internet censorship and identify dissidents. The 2018 Cybersecurity Law requires tech companies to store data locally and hand over user data. The '10,000-person cyber unit' (Force 47) combines human trolls with automated systems to manipulate public opinion. Hundreds of bloggers and activists are imprisoned for their online speech.
actors_en: Vietnamese government / Ministry of Public Security

timeline_en.title_en: Force 47: 10,000-person cyber unit activated
timeline_en.description_en: Vietnam reveals the existence of Force 47 — a 10,000-strong cyber unit that monitors social media platforms for government-critical content and manipulates public opinion with coordinated campaigns. The unit uses automated tools to identify and flag critical posts.

timeline_en.title_en: Cybersecurity Law: data localization and censorship
timeline_en.description_en: The Cybersecurity Law takes effect. Facebook and Google must store user data on Vietnamese servers and remove government-critical content on request within 24 hours. Facebook later admits to having complied with Vietnamese government censorship demands in 2020 and restricted content.

timeline_en.title_en: Facebook censors on Vietnam's orders
timeline_en.description_en: Facebook confirms that it has restricted government-critical content in Vietnam after the government threatened to take its servers offline. The company blocks content critical of the regime and restricts access to pages of human rights organizations. Vietnam becomes a test case for authoritarian control over global platforms.

timeline_en.title_en: More than 150 political prisoners for online speech
timeline_en.description_en: Vietnam holds more than 150 people in prison for online speech — the highest number in Southeast Asia. RSF ranks Vietnam 178 out of 180 on press freedom. Despite international criticism, surveillance is expanding: Vietnam orders TikTok to remove 'anti-state' content and invests in its own AI censorship capabilities.

xinjiang-ueberwachung.json.description_en: Mass surveillance of the Uyghur population in the Chinese region of Xinjiang through AI-powered systems. Facial recognition, movement tracking, and predictive analysis are used to surveil, categorize, and intern millions of people in re-education camps.

timeline_en.title_en: Construction of the surveillance infrastructure
timeline_en.description_en: China begins the massive expansion of surveillance infrastructure in Xinjiang. Hundreds of thousands of cameras with facial recognition are installed, checkpoints with biometric capture are set up, and Wi-Fi sniffers are deployed in public spaces.

timeline_en.title_en: Integrated Joint Operations Platform (IJOP)
timeline_en.description_en: The Integrated Joint Operations Platform is introduced, combining data from surveillance cameras, Wi-Fi tracking, smartphone scans, and police reports. The system automatically generates lists of people classified as suspicious.

timeline_en.title_en: Mass internment begins
timeline_en.description_en: Based on AI-driven surveillance data, an estimated one to two million Uyghurs and other Turkic Muslims are interned in so-called re-education camps. The AI system identifies people as risks based on criteria such as prayer behavior, contacts abroad, or smartphone use.

timeline_en.title_en: China Cables and international documentation
timeline_en.description_en: Leaked internal documents (China Cables) document systematic mass internment and the role of AI surveillance. International media and NGOs document the scale of the repression.

timeline_en.title_en: Sanctions and genocide designation
timeline_en.description_en: Several Western governments, including the US, classify the treatment of Uyghurs as genocide. Sanctions are imposed on Chinese officials and involved technology companies such as Hikvision. The UN releases a report confirming severe human rights violations.
